utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. You're continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Maslic. Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will continue where we left it off yesterday, and I will put you a follow-up question, a follow-up question to the questions of Judge Lindholm, where you said that the Bosna River was the separation line, separating two warring sides. Can you tell me: What were the two warring sides that the Bosna River divided?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The separation line divided the HVO forces and the HV forces, on one side, and on the other side were the forces of our army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have also said that this was organised exclusively by the Red Cross, and this is what distinguished this exchange. The later exchanges in which you participated, were they also organised by the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the International Red Cross did not organise these later exchanges but did participate in them, as a general rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you in fact, during those exchanges, get to know the principals that the International Red Cross used to organise those exchanges? Was that the first time that you had an opportunity to familiarise yourself with them?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, the witness said that the International Red Cross did not organise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Your microphone. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Lindholm, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: On side number 1, line 23, the last words are: "Of our army." What do you mean by that expression? Because your community was a mixed community. What do you mean by "our army"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had in mind the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, you were raising a point. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. My microphone wasn't working before. It is now, and I apologise. Furthermore, I understand that we don't have our LiveNote working, and if that could be rectified, that would assist us. But in any event, my objection was simply that the witness said that it wasn't organised by the International Red Cross. And then I think Mr. Lukic put to the witness, within a question or two -- yes: "Did you in fact during those exchanges get to know how the principals that the International Red Cross used to organise those exchanges?" Now, that's incorrect. The witness said they weren't, they were organised locally and the Red Cross participated. So that's important to note and I request that Mr. Lukic phrase his questions in such a way that it follows what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. And maybe the technical booth can assist you with your laptops. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is an interpretation mistake. I asked the witness about the later exchanges, and by that I meant the ones that followed that first exchange. And then I asked the witness whether in those later exchanges the principles that they had learned from the International Red Cross were used. I will tell you what the witness said yesterday, page 26, line 21 [In English]: [Previous translation continues] ... "to get involved in the first exchange." [Interpretation] And then, on page 77, line 11: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... sorry. [No interpretation] [In English] Local Red Cross organisation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. We don't seem to be getting translation here into English. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm not receiving any either, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think it should be all right now. Maybe you can start again, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat what I have quoted. I will now quote from page 77, which is important to me, due to the objection from the Prosecutor. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... "attended to that exchange, and she asked for the local Red Cross chapter to also be involved in the activity in order to help her."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. We don't have any person's name. Is this the person that the witness yesterday was calling Ms. Katherine or Ms. Kathy? Because it isn't coming up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were explaining this yesterday, you had in mind Ms. Katherine from the International Red Cross, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And she is the person that organised that first exchange?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And after that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. Just to get it clear. Now with this question, your question: "And she is the person that organised that first exchange"? I think this the point that Mr. Di Fazio has just raised. Was it the International Committee of the Red Cross who organised the exchange or was it the local personnel, the local Red Cross? And I think that's what we need to get clear here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was about to clarify that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that first exchange that took place in Zasavica along the banks of the river in Zasavica, who organised that first exchange?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first exchange on the River of Bosna in the village of Zasavica was organised by the International Red Cross, personally by Ms. Katherine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If I could just ask a subsidiary question to that. If it was organised by Ms. Katherine for the International Committee of the Red Cross and she was on the side of the border in Bosanski Samac area, who was her counterpart? Was there another person acting for the International Committee of the Red Cross on the other side of the border?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, what she said was that she had contacted the representatives from Odzak and arranged this. Who did she arrange the mechanism of the exchange, I don't know, but I know what she asked from the local Red Cross in Samac, and I know that we abided by her requests and acted pursuant to her requests to provide everything that was necessary for that exchange, and by that I am first and foremost implying the medical team, stretchers, ambulance vehicles, a boat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Lukic, for intervening once again, but I think it might be important for us to know who Ms. Katherine exactly was. Presumably, if she was a representative of the ICRC, we would have more details about her than simply to know that she was Ms. Kathy or Ms. Katherine. Presumably the ICRC in Geneva would have her on their books and we would have some more knowledge. Not to ask this witness that, but I think it would be important to have more information than just "Ms. Katherine, Ms. Kathy."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be very pleased, Your Honour, if the Defence were in the position to give you more information. In the pre-trial stage we had some issues raised regarding the International Red Cross, and that had to do with the arrest of Stevan Todorovic. And at the time, the International Red Cross delivered certain documents in which they informed that they were not authorised to provide any further evidence. I will ask the witness about that and about other individuals that had to do with the Red Cross and that the witness will mention in his further testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything further about Ms. Katherine? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I'd ask the witness not answer that question just at the moment. This issue is a matter that the Prosecution intended to address you upon at the close of the examination-in-chief and before the cross-examination started, and having now been raised, it would be in the Prosecution's view an opportune moment a good moment to address you on this very issue. And I would like to do so, if you permit us to do so. Mr. Re will address you on it, in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But why don't we proceed with the evidence of the witness and conclude? Because the witness knows some information and his counsel will lead him. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, certainly. I'm talking about the issue of the presence of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I know. Because it's part of the evidence of this witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Would you just give me a moment to confer with my colleague, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I only raise it because Judge Williams has herself raised the issue of the role of the International Red Cross in this particular exchange and the information available to the parties, and it's because of that that the very issue that we intended to address you on has arisen all of a sudden in the course of the examination-in-chief. So that's the reason why I raised the idea of addressing you now rather than when we had intended to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. I think it's better not to interrupt the evidence of the witness. Let the examination-in-chief come to an end. You can then raise it. If it will require reopening the examination-in-chief, fine. MR. DI FAZIO: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Otherwise if it's a matter that you can deal with in cross-examination, fine. MR. DI FAZIO: It's a matter of submission, not a matter that I can deal with in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Let's finish the examination-in-chief of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, do you have any additional information concerning Ms. Katherine? Where was she from? Did she provide any additional information to you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have very little information on that lady. I had at the time -- all I know is that she said that her office was in Tuzla and that it covered this area as well. And she was particularly interested in fulfilling her humanitarian mission in that area, in Posavina and in Samac. I don't know anything else concerning her.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also said that the contacts were established between the representatives of Odzak and Samac, since there was a separation line running there, what were these contacts about? Do you know what were the contents? Did it have to do with the ceasefire?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it did not pertain to the ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now we will go back to another issue, but also remain within that same period of time. The month of May is quite important for our case, due to numerous events. You've mentioned the events in Odzak municipality in May of 1992. We will not go into details, but do you personally know what was the attitude of Mr. Tadic with respect to the events surrounding the Serbs there? Did he have any clear personal attitude regarding that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned then that Mr. Tadic was born in Novi Grad and that he had a lot of relatives there, close relatives. And he inquired about his relatives who lived in Novi Grad and who, according to the information received, were imprisoned then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information concerning some other activities about the lists of the Red Cross that were sent to Belgrade and that pertained the events in Odzak? Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Tadic at the time went to Belgrade several times, to the Red Cross of Yugoslavia and some other places. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm not objecting, but it should be made clear, I think, that -- yes. The lists of the Red Cross that were sent to Belgrade. Is the witness talking about the local Red Cross or again the International Committee of the Red Cross? And indeed, throughout the evidence of this witness, whenever possible, if Mr. Lukic could assist by making it absolutely clear which particular Red Cross the witness is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think my learned colleague and I will devote particular attention to this, but so far whenever I refer to the Red Cross, I always meant the local chapter. When I meant the International Red Cross, I always accentuated that particular fact. But we will be precise hence forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So please tell us who organised this and how were these lists compiled? What were these lists? Who organised the compiling of these lists? Who were they sent to, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I heard that Mr. Tadic had gone to see the people in the Red Cross of Yugoslavia with lists of Serbs who had been captured in Odzak municipality. Whether he went also to the international -- to the committee of the International Red Cross in Belgrade, that I don't know. What I do know is that he went several times in a bid to seek assistance for the release of the Serbs who had been captured in Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We shall stick to the subject of relations between the International Red Cross and the local Red Cross. After this first exchange - and I will also revert to that subject in a bit more detail later - do you remember about the activities of the International Red Cross? Who came there from this organisation? Who did they see? Who did they meet with and what did they do there?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this exchange, I did not see this Ms. Katherine, nor did she come to the local Red Cross chapter. I heard that she had left the area. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Maslic, was this Ms. Katherine acting all alone or was she accompanied by other persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can recall, she came alone in a Red Cross vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That was actually going to be -- my second question was going to be: How do you know that she was an official representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that because this is how she introduced herself, and she had a vehicle with the marks of the International Red Cross, and she had her business card, which also had the International Red Cross identification mark on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To follow up on the question of Her Honour Judge Williams, did she have an interpreter? Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot recall that she had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you started telling us about the other visits. Who came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic. Just following up on your question, then. If she didn't have an interpreter, Mr. Maslic, was she able to speak in your language to you? Could she speak in Bosnian, Serbian, Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She could speak Serbian. She could speak Serbian, nothing to write home about, but we could manage. I could understand what she was saying to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please continue.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this exchange, I don't know how much time had precisely elapsed, but in my assessment it was quite soon thereafter, a new delegate of the International Committee of the Red Cross came. As far as I can recollect, his name was Matheas Kind or something like that. He had an interpreter. This was a lady by the name of Snjezana, I believe. They had offices -- an office, rather, in Bijeljina. And he came to the local Red Cross chapter proposing to offer assistance, the assistance that he was able to offer us. So during this first encounter, he clarified the role of the International Red Cross and he told us that he would exert efforts within the framework of his mandate and his competencies, so as to render assistance to the citizens, to the citizens who had found themselves in this war-ridden area. He also asked us to get involved as much as possible. That means the local Red Cross people, to draw up adequate lists of people, of citizens who needed help, and added that he would, on his part, attempt to organise the supply of humanitarian relief supplies to the area of Samac municipality as soon as possible. He asked me whether we were receiving, whether we had received any relief supplies from any other agency, and I responded that we had received help from the Red Cross of Yugoslavia. He asked me what was peculiar to the situation in Samac. In view of the fact that the town was partially surrounded, there was a partial encirclement around it, and there was a very small pass, a corridor, through Brcko, and as there were very -- there was very frequent fighting going on there, I told him that what was characteristic, what was peculiar to the situation in Samac was that in Samac we had a chemo-dialysis centre and that we had specific problems in that respect, and also that we had problems -- that our citizens had a problem to communicate with anyone without the area, meaning outside the area of the municipality. He then said to me that he would seek to get involved in all these activities, to help us, and he also told me that the International Committee of the Red Cross had already prepared forms, model forms, through which messages were to be sent, and letters. He explained this in some detail to my associates, namely, that people who had been instructed how they were to write their messages, briefly, succinctly, how they were to be addressed, and who was the actual sender, and that all these data should be indicated, and he explained this in some detail. On that occasion he gave us several hundred of such model forms. After that, on the local Radio Samac, we broadcast that there existed a possibility for all those wishing to communicate, to write to members of their families or to their relatives who had remained outside the area or in different parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina or Croatia, or in the broader area, generally speaking. So after we broadcast this information, people came to the Red Cross office to get these forms. They filled them in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, details, please, are not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us - it's obviously quite clear to the Trial Chamber that they came there to fill in those forms - just tell us: Who were they given to after having been filled in?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The filled-in forms remained in the local chapter of the Red Cross. They would be collected there. And Mr. Matheas came there initially two times a week and later once a week, depending on the actual need. He took all these messages and transmitted them to the other side and he brought them from the other side, from Tuzla, from Sarajevo. He brought like messages from other sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me: Do you know whether these messages which he brought there, what was their content, as a rule? What did people say and what did people write to the people in your area? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually did not examine the content of those messages. I myself wrote in this way to my own relatives. What I was primarily interested in was, of course, what the situation was like where they were and how life was, and things like that. But after this communication link via messages written in this way had been established, I talked to people, and they told me that -- said that people were asking to see them, that their people were asking to see them, for them to come to Gradacac, to Tuzla, to Croatia, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you yesterday, and you have already made some reference to this, but now I will repeat. Mr. Maslic, did you know that there was a detention unit or that there were detention units in Samac, and where were they?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about those. I heard about detentions, about people having been detained, and according to the information I received in the Territorial Defence Staff and the elementary school and the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go to these institutions while the detainees were being held there?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went into any of those buildings during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that any of your colleagues from the local Red Cross chapter ever went to these institutions?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Our volunteers are activists, went to the Red Cross. I apologise. I apologise. Went to the prison. They carried messages there which had been brought by Mr. Matheas. And even though he himself, as far as I had been informed, would personally deliver those messages to people in the detention units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. This is my next question: Do you know whether Mr. Matheas, or anybody else from the International Red Cross, ever visited these detention units? Do you have any direct or indirect knowledge of that, so that we could expedite matters?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not talk about this with Mr. Matheas. As far as I know, he had talks conducted in the police, where he asked for permission to go there, and also to conduct some of the activities that he was conducting. But I do know that the activists of the local Red Cross chapter did go there and that they delivered food, and also a medical team would go there, would go there to these prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, again no objection, but it would be a matter of some use to the Prosecution if we could have any names of people who, if the witness can tell us, of course, of these Red Cross activists who delivered food to the prisoners. It might assist us, and of course it will assist you to know, because the names might have cropped up before in the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my learned colleague. This is exactly what I was going to ask. Perhaps this is the right time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So do you know which one of the local Red Cross activists went to the detention units?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Vasovic, Svetozar went there; Mrs. Mirka Petkovic; Mrs. Anka Jovanovic. I know that they went to the detention units. And as far as the medical crews are concerned, as far as I can remember, I believe Dr. Stanimirovic went there, the lady doctor, Ruza Brdar Masic, and a doctor whose surname I believe was Fajcinovic, and some other staff also, whose names I do not know, but these were the people that I talked to on that particular score doing the work for the local Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know about any beatings taking place in these units? Did anyone tell you about any beatings going on in those units?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from these activists that people had been beaten and that there were traces of beating on the persons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you talk about this with Mr. Matheas? Did he tell you, did he convey to you any of his observations in that particular respect?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Matheas did not wish to talk about this. He told me that he was aware of what the extent of the powers of the local Red Cross chapter were but that within his own mandate and the International Red Cross, he would undertake everything in his power for these people to be protected and for these people not to be tormented. What he actually did do is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now something that has to do with our previous topic, the messages and the searches.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender a few documents. The first one has the internal marking PDB 38/3. It is entitled "The list of persons who are sought by the Red Cross of Samac, June --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters missed the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you repeat the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 5th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Lukic, in the English version that we have, the English is "list of missing persons"." I take it it's the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. That's the same document, with that translation. And I will now read out the original in B/C/S. "The list of persons who are to be traced."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, are you familiar with this particular document, or in general with this kind of documents? Who issued this document, and what is the purpose of this document?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, it's somewhat leading, that question. It's already -- because it assumes there were a series of documents. We should be clear, first of all, if this is the only such document that exists or whether or not there were a series of such documents, many of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The way the question was put is like this is just one of -- MR. DI FAZIO: It assumes that. It assumes that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure you'll clear that up. MR. DI FAZIO: That should not be an assumption that is made and we need to have that clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't want to put a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, can you please tell us: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started saying that I was familiar with this document and that this wasn't an only document. Almost daily, lists similar to this one were compiled, and at the time we used to read out these lists on the local radio so that the families called or contacted, from the other side, through written messages and inquired about their relatives or friends, and people in this way were traced through the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like this document to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We received yesterday that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. We were told that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D90/3 and D90/3 ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The following document has an internal mark PDB 52/3. It is somewhat longer, but we will cover it quite quickly. This is a letter with attached document from the Serb Red Cross of Modrica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] PDB 52/3, dated 12th of September, 1992. It has several pages, 11 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this document. I think that you were shown this document when we were preparing your testimony. Do you know this document from before?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document, and we had similar documents from other municipalities. We tried to supply to the municipality of Modrica, Doboj, Brcko, Bijeljina, and other municipalities similar lists so that they would be familiar with our lists and so that we could try and resolve the tracing requests that had come in. So this is just one document in a series of similar documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Once the exchanges started, were similar documents supplied to the other side, and did you have any communication with the other side concerning missing persons?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the only mode of communication with the other side was through written messages. Once the contact was established and once the meetings started, then these lists became a daily routine, so that we would receive replies, send in requests, and this was exchanged between our side and the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can see here that this document is addressed to the Serb Red Cross of Bosanski Samac, and underneath it said: "To the service for tracing and exchange." Tell me, please, but very briefly: How many different services existed within your local Red Cross? Tell me, please, that. How many different services you had within your local Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already talked about this yesterday. I said that we had several services organised. One was the humanitarian aid service, the other one was for the distribution of the aid. Then we had a tracing service and the medical service. We called them services.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what you told us yesterday. Now, please take a look at this document. And we can see that there are names of some persons here. Can you tell us, please, about their ethnic background. Are there members of all three nations here?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There are members of all three nations here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we get a number for this document? I would like it to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D91/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now turn to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that you had been told by your neighbours something about people wearing multicoloured clothing. Did you hear, while living in Samac, about people who had come from outside? Do you know how they got to Samac? Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about them. We called them multicoloured members of special units. They were very arrogant. They were armed. They had no insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know anyone by name among those?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Lugar, with whom I personally had a problem. He threatened me, telling me that what we were doing was done only in the interests of Croats and Muslims, not in the interest of Serbs. And he told me that such a Red Cross should not exist in wartime. However, after the people who knew me intervened, they told him who I was and he stopped threatening me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, tell me, please: Did you hear about a crime of his, or any crime committed in May in the territory of Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about that. It took place in the village of Crkvina. A terrible crime was committed there. Several people who had been imprisoned were killed. But this story was spread out through the town out of fear. I couldn't hear this officially from anyone. This was mentioned in talks in town. But there was fear among people. I personally feared this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when did this take place? When did you hear about this? A month later, two months later, three months later?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact date, but we heard about this shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now ask you a question that has to do with the victims in Crkvina. Do you know, do you have any direct knowledge concerning the fact that Miroslav Tadic, later on, got involved in finding the bodies of these people? And if you know that it is so, do you know the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Tadic got involved in this matter. He attempted to find the bodies of these people who had been killed. He probably contacted representatives of Odzak municipality, and together they looked for these bodies. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, you should be clear about this evidence, whether the witness is saying this -- that Mr. Tadic did in fact, as a matter of reality, contact representatives of the Odzak municipality and with them looked for the bodies, or whether he is speculating. He said he probably did this. It's not clear to me from the use of that expression, whether that's -- he's surmising or thinking or suggesting that might have happened or whether he's saying: Yes, it did happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, if you know this: When was this? When was it that Mr. Tadic made these attempts, and what do you know about these attempts of Mr. Tadic in trying to find these bodies?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Tadic had radio connection with the representatives from Odzak and that after some time - I don't know exactly how long, perhaps two or three months after that - he received a request from the representatives of Odzak to try and find these bodies. I know that he attempted to locate the bodies. I know about this. I'm not supposing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in 1994 he made some other attempts concerning this at the level of the republic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The entire course of negotiations and contacts -- through the entire course of negotiations and contacts with the other side, this request was repeated continuously by the representatives from Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we've mentioned Lugar and others, I will ask you about another person. Have you heard about Captain Jez?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. He's an officer who worked in the brigade command as a security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the commander of the brigade when this man was the security officer?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was the commander. I can't speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was close to Lugar and Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what his relationship with Lugar and Todorovic was, so I can't speak about that, because I had no opportunity to establish direct contact with the three of them. Therefore, I can't speak about any possible cooperation or their relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you an eyewitness to an incident with Captain Jez concerning the lists of people who were to be exchanged and who were sought?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. But before I answer your question, let me just tell you that all of the lists of people who were sought by the other side were sent to the police, and the security officer in the brigade, in order that it could be verified whether there was any hindrance for these people to be exchanged, whether there was perhaps a criminal complaint against these people. I remember a list that went up to Captain Jez. He looked at it and sent it back, crossing out the names of all of the people who were supposed to come from Odzak through the exchange and who had the same last name as Mr. Tadic. When we inquired why was it done, we received a reply that: We have plenty of Tadics here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could now the witness be shown document P71.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: What, in your opinion, are vital facilities, facilities of key importance?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion -- MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if Your Honours please, his opinion is neither here nor there and not relevant, and he shouldn't give his opinion. We're here to listen to his evidence of facts. And secondly, if he doesn't know, never seen the document before, what's the purpose of his commenting on it? He can certainly give evidence about anything that he might know about isolation of Croats and so on, but an analysis of the document itself is it not something that he should embark on if he's never seen it before and doesn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm astounded at this position of the Prosecution. Many witnesses of the Prosecution have also never seen this document. But Mr. Di Fazio has asked what vital facilities were. I have to ask the witness what something is in order to establish whether something had happened or not. I fail to comprehend this intervention. If I want to ask -- if my intention is to ask the witness whether what is written in the document indeed happened, the witness can say that something did not happen, but he doesn't know what the concept that we are talking about is in the document in question. Of course, I can rephrase my question, if that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the -- yes. The Trial Chamber is of the view that perhaps the only mistake was asking for his opinion, because it is normal that a document might not have been seen by a witness, but when he reads it, he might know of the incidents that are discussed in the document, so he can be asked about that. MR. DI FAZIO: I've got no objection to that at all. I'm quite happy for him to be asked about isolation or if he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's the opinion that -- yes. He shouldn't give his opinion. MR. DI FAZIO: -- talk about things that he saw and heard. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to construct the question in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What are vital facilities?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to give you my opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. I want you to tell me what vital facilities in Samac are.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The health centre, the hospital, the silo, the school. So these are the vital facilities in Samac, those which are facilities of common interest and significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But do you know -- do you know that at any time during the war, any of these facilities of the kind that you have just mentioned were -- that any person of Croat nationality was taken to any such facility and put there?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen anyone brought there and put there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me something else: Do you have any information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, but when the witness said that he had never seen any Croat, and so on, brought into those vital facilities, does it mean that he wasn't in -- he hadn't the possibility of seeing it, or that nobody brought into those facilities? There is a great difference between those two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally see, did you hear from anyone, did you receive any information about that whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in Samac throughout that period and I moved around town quite freely. And I know the locations of all these facilities, which I have enumerated. So I never saw anyone on those facilities placed there in this way. People used these institutions. They went in, they passed by. They used these institutions, such as the hospital, for instance. I never saw that anyone or heard that anyone had been placed upon such a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just to go back to my colleague Judge Lindholm's question, though. There is a difference between seeing and knowing, and even in the second answer by Mr. Maslic, there still seems to be a little confusion on that as to -- even though he didn't see, did he know? So just to have a very simple answer. Did Mr. Maslic know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And secondly -- I withdraw the question. I was about to say: Even with respect to the school. It isn't said here whether it's the secondary or the elementary school. But your answer was no, so I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, do you have any knowledge to the effect that in the month of May, any people were taken away to any place in an organised fashion from Samac municipality territory, and why?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt in May that a group had been taken away from town, a group of Muslims and Croats who had been taken to Crkvina, to the culture centre, and Crkvina is a nearby village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the mix of this population like, and do you perhaps know their actual number?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were between 100 and 150 persons in the group, and these were mostly Croats and Muslims. There were also children among them, and elderly and infirm -- and sick people. At the time, we in the local Red Cross intervened immediately, and our activists, and I personally also saw to it that these people would get the basic necessities, starting with food and toiletries, the basic hygienic supplies. But I know that I was there only for a short while, perhaps five or six days -- they were there, sorry, between five or six days and then they were returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear who had led them away? How had this been organised?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that had been done by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: When you came there and saw these people, were they being secured in any way?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were being guarded by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to these people after these five or six days?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, they were returned home. Because our activists went there after that time and they saw that they had already gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you inquire why these people had been taken there?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why they had been taken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'll leave behind this month of May period. But just a brief question associated with the Prosecution's case. Do you know Mr. Osman Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him by sight. I believe that he was a merchant, a shop assistant. He worked in the old supermarket.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether he was exchanged as part of the May exchange in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is not that material. Did you know his wife?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did you know where it was that he had gone to after the exchange?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, have you ever told anyone, did you ever tell anyone of the civilians who came to you and reported that they wished to be exchanged that they could not be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never told anything of the kind to anyone, nor could I have said anything like that to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear, while working on these activities associated with the exchange, did you ever hear Miroslav Tadic ever tell anyone that that person could not be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had never heard anything of the kind personally, nor had I ever heard anything like that told to me by my associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I should like to tender a number of other documents for us to examine the other activities of the Red Cross. On the basis of these documents, we shall try to expedite matters. The first document that I'm interested in is PDB 43/3, internal mark, I shall repeat, PDB 43/3, confirmation or receipt of the certificate of the Red Cross of 18th of August, 1992. All these documents are self-explanatory. All these documents which follow, and we will not dwell on them at length.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've already said, this document is self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it the practice of the Red Cross to issue certificates of this kind? How frequently? And tell me specifically: In these cases, what were the nationalities of the persons to whom they were issued, and what was the next step?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These certificates were issued with the objective of enabling the person in question to move around the area unhindered. Specifically, this is a person who is from the Red Cross, Fikreta Omeragic, a Muslim by ethnicity, and she was going to Belgrade to visit her husband in hospital who had been wounded in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We shall not go into those details. Just tell me: The last sentence, the last line, I should read it, applies with the pass issued of the station of public security of Bosanski Samac. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every citizen had to have a pass issued by the public security station in order to be able to leave the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So with just this certificate a person could not go on a trip?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not with just this certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document please be tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D92/3 and D92/3 ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document that I wish to examine bears the internal mark PDB 66/3. It is also a Red Cross document from the Red Cross of Samac, from the 28th of November, 1992. It is a list, an inventory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know this document?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I'm familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, just very briefly: What was the role of the Red Cross in connection with this document? Why was it compiled in the first place? Very briefly, not the entire story, please. It is self-explanatory also.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see from the content of the document what it is -- what its subject is. So these were jewels deposited for custody with the commercial bank to be kept in the vault of the commercial bank until the return of the lady in question from hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what is established here? What is this in handwriting, written in handwriting, in the top right corner?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That she had indeed taken her -- recovered her jewellery upon returning from hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Of what ethnicity was this lady?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we also tender this document into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D93/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The internal mark of the next document is PDB 87/3, and it is a letter dated 30th January, 1993, written by Jovo Lakic, a priest, and addressed to the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document is self-explanatory one as well. Just tell me: Was it the practice for institutions to address you and offer their assistance in tracing, or what was the practice like?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not infrequent at all for representatives of both organisations and for individuals to themselves address the Red Cross with either a request for them to be assisted or to be given information, and there were also those who offered their assistance to us. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, just a matter for the transcript. Mr. Lukic asked: Was it the practice for - something - he said something - institutions to address you, and I didn't hear it, nor does it come out in the transcript, in English, anyway. Did Mr. Lukic refer to a particular type of institution in the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I said various institutions, different institutions, because it is quite clear from this document -- in this specific case what institution is in question. This is the Samac parish. And so this is in this document, and so my question was whether other, different institutions addressed the Red Cross in this way, with the same intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell me briefly: Here different villages are mentioned, Samac, Grebnice, Novo Selo, et cetera. Are these villages in which both Serbs and Croats lived in the surroundings of Samac?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Grebnice, for instance. This is generally known there was such a village.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are inhabited places here which were inhabited by Serbs and Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I be assigned a number for this document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D94/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Maslic. I'm just wondering: When you got such letters from institutions, and in this case from a religious person, a priest, Jovo Lakic, was it usual that they would say, as it does in the English translation: Information was wanted from "camps run by the Ustashas or other enemies"? Was the language usually put in those types of ways?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was not the general practice, no. But different terminology was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Maslic: Did the Red Cross have anything to do with what is known as children's allowances, and what were, what are, children's allowances and benefits?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, the Red Cross had nothing to do with the children's benefits, but the service of the social work centre did. So these were allowances which, until the outbreak of the war, used to be paid out to families who had children up to 3 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please show the witness document PDB 5/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Is it blue or yellow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can go ahead, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document is also self-explanatory. Did the Red Cross issue certificates like these? You don't have to go into any detail. Just tell me: This is obviously a document from the early period in the war. Until what time did this possibility of receiving so-called baby packages exist?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't finished. May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war operations, there were no payments made in money. Everything was in kind. The Red Cross, as an organisation, a humanitarian organisation, had, as part of the humanitarian relief supplies that it had received from the Red Cross of Yugoslavia and the International Committee of the Red Cross, also had some baby passes, baby packages, which contained the basic necessities for a newborn infant. In addition to these, we also had toiletries, hygienic supplies, baby formulas, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please, just tell me: These are two different certificates. You can see by the serial numbers. What persons -- what nationality were the persons who were given these packages, parcels, rather?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first certificate, it is a Muslim surname, but I do not know whether the lady in question was a Croat or Serbian. Jelica. But in the other certificate, Almira Arapovic is certainly Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please be assigned a number for this document, and I believe it would be a convenient time for us to take a break after that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D95/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break until 1615 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, we will now turn to a completely different topic, a topic of great interest to us. Mr. Maslic, can you tell us, briefly: What are exchanges? Can you tell us: What principles were used in the course of exchanges? And in the first place, why did the exchanges start?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the first part of my testimony, I said several times something about exchanges. But now I will answer directly your question. An exchange is a process by which people cross from one side to the other. And when I say "sides," I'm referring to the warring sides, or rather, this is an exchange of imprisoned soldiers. Exchange is a mechanism enabling the soldiers who had been captured to cross to the other side. The exchange itself comes after negotiations between the warring sides, in the process of which they agree upon the names of persons who wish to cross over or the names of persons who are sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... not understand what is written in the transcript. It's on page 34, line 23, last two words, warring -- if the witness could repeat his answer. Warring sides. That's what I heard, but I don't want to put --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes. Sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe that you said that there were two sides. Can you tell us: What were those two sides?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Warring sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Maybe we ought to know from the witness, Mr. Lukic, which word the warring sides from the perspective of the exchanges that he is familiar with? MR. DI FAZIO: And if I may just add something to -- which arises from Your Honour's question. It's not a terribly important point, and I -- but the witness isn't an expert on -- he seems to be talking generally about exchanges. I've got no problem at all with him describing what he saw and observed in 1992 and indeed the evidence should be -- you should hear the evidence, of course, and I encourage it, but the way it's being framed at the moment, it sounds as if it's a rather general discussion on exchanges generally, and I don't think this witness is entitled to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. I will clarify. What you're saying now, you are telling us based on personal experience and the information you gained personally while you worked on those tasks. Can you please explain to Her Honour Judge Williams: What were the two warring sides throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By "warring sides," I mean Serbs on one side, and on the other side Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there had been any exchanges between Muslims and Croats, in cases where the conflict was between those two sides?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you again. When you are talking about sides, geographically there are many sides. One, for instance, Bosnia-Herzegovina; and on the other side of Sava River, Croatia. And other sides, what does the witness mean with "sides," "warring sides"? And then a follow-up question. I can't find it here now on the transcript, but he gave me an impression that persons exchanged were soldiers kept in prisons, or wherever, and that doesn't fit in with what we have heard earlier in this case, that most of the people exchanged were civilians. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness did explain what he meant by "warring sides" at 36, 7, that it meant Serbs on one side; and on the other side, Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: But where was the line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now speak in greater detail about the exchange of civilians and the exchange of imprisoned individuals, because these are different categories, and the witness will clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: What comes before the exchange, according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to carry out an exchange of imprisoned soldiers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Are we again dealing with the matters the witness witnessed relevant to this case or is he giving a general definition?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm putting very specific questions concerning the exchanges in which the witness participated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, the exchanges in which you participated, can you tell us what precedes an exchange? Let's take, for example, the one that took place in September of 1992 in Dragalic. Did you participate in that particular exchange?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak about this as a representative of the Red Cross. I can speak about the concept of an exchange. Negotiations precede any exchange. Negotiations between representatives of warring sides. On one side, there would usually be a committee of the Serb side and on the other side there would normally be a committee representing the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, let's stop for a second, please? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, we're running into precisely the problem that I foreshadowed. You see the witness is saying -- for example, the witness says negotiations proceed in the exchange, negotiations between representatives of warring sides. One is left wondering whether the witness is talking generally about exchanges or is he talking about what he saw and heard and observed, or at least was reported to him? And it's that that we have to be absolutely clear about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think we have to go back to specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to put this line of questions because this applies to absolutely all of the exchanges in which this witness participated. So I did not want to repeat that this was typical for every exchange. And then later on I wanted to go into details concerning each particular exchange. I think that this would facilitate the appropriate explanation of what comes under the term "exchange."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. As long as we understand it the way you've put it, that he is discussing what went on, what he witnessed, what he did, or what others did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, what do you know concerning the negotiations in which you participated? What did you normally ask from the other side during the negotiations in which you participated? I assume that you participated in some negotiations between 1992 and 1993. What did you normally ask for from the other side? Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to tell you first something generally about the exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. Please tell us something about the exchanges in which you participated.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a general rule, there was only an exchange of imprisoned soldiers. The Red Cross, as a humanitarian organisation, got involved and took part in these negotiations in order to enable the civilians who wanted to cross over to the other side to cross at the same time when some of their family members were exchanged as soldiers. We attempted to honour the principle of unification of families. Your Honours, you are probably familiar with the fact that citizens of Samac municipality had family members living in the Republic of Croatia, which was quite nearby. Those people lived in Odzak, in Gradacac, in Sarajevo, and other places. During those negotiations which were conducted by military committees, we, using the records kept by the Red Cross, the records listing the citizens who wished to cross over to the other side, I mean crossing to the side held by the other warring side, because this was an only mode for them to go to the other side and unite with their families. So we attempted to honour or to grant these requests of citizens every time when there was an exchange of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Civilians who wanted to cross over to the other side, where did they apply for this?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that citizens received written messages in the Red Cross premises through the International Red Cross and that they received information concerning their family members who had remained on the other side, they would come to the Red Cross, apply to be exchanged, stating where they wished to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. So, Mr. Maslic, you mentioned on page 39, lines 3 to 5, that the Red Cross was enabling civilians who wanted to cross over to the other side to cross at the same time when some of their family members were exchanged as soldiers. By "soldiers," are you referring to prisoners of war? If you know that, I'd appreciate your answering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I mean prisoners of war. But that fell under the jurisdiction of -- exclusive jurisdiction of military committees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: But did you have any records which indicated which civilians had family members who were prisoner of war soldiers who were going to cross over? You presumably had to try to bring two lists together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were such records of civilians who had applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To follow up on Judge Williams's question: In your cooperation -- while you were cooperating with the military committees, did you know who was to be exchanged through a military exchange? For example, who was to be exchanged from Batkovici, for example?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A military committee that existed within the corps of the army of Republika Srpska, there was one such committee in Banja Luka. It was attached to the 1st Krajina Corps. And the other one was in Bijeljina, and it was within the East Bosnian Corps. All citizens from Samac municipality who had been captured as soldiers and kept in prison in Batkovic were put on a list and the military committee gave us a list of such individuals with respect to whom negotiations had been conducted to exchange them, or rather, to free them. And based on that list and the list of citizens that had applied to the Red Cross, we compiled a list in order to enable them to cross to the other side without hindrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And to follow up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you again. When you are talking about exchange and the other side, is this, so to say, meaning Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the south, and Croatia in the north, or in which direction? Exchange, other side, and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The concept of a warring side presupposes, on the one hand, vis-a-vis Croatia; and on the other side, on the other hand, vis-a-vis a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, namely, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "the federation," you mean under the jurisdiction of the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were territories which were exclusively under the control of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can later take a map, if need be, to clearly indicate the places in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: So exchanges took place both up to the north, over the Sava River, and to the south, into the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So to follow up on your previous explanation: There were some persons who had been taken prisoner in Batkovic, and because of some decisions were not exchanged when their family members were exchanged. Did you actually accommodate the requests of these people who wanted to leave, irrespective of where their spouses, for instance, were?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not set any conditions on anyone. There were some families. No family members of which had been taken prisoner as a soldier were not imprisoned in Batkovic. But before the war, a family member of such families had perhaps gone to Croatia, to work there or because he had relatives there, so that the families were separated in that way. So we placed no conditions on anyone. But we always tried, when it came to people -- persons who had been imprisoned as soldiers, if they stated that it was their desire to cross over to the other side, we always sought to make it possible for them and to make it possible for their families as well, which is to say spouses, children, to be able to cross over together with them. This is mainly what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained that civilians came to the local Red Cross, where they reported that they wished to be exchanged, and on such occasions I believe you would compile lists of the people who reported.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every person who reported to the Red Cross on any grounds whatsoever, whether they sought some sort of assistance or wanted to have a message delivered written, or any person wishing to be enabled to leave the territory, we made lists of all such persons, and records of all such persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the document with the internal mark PDB 133/3 be shown to the witness. This is entitled "List of persons who have applied to cross over to the opposite side by reason of family reunification."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please take a look at this document and tell us whether these were -- these are indeed the lists that were made by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are such lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the state of Croatia making the entry of civilians into its territory conditional upon anything? Did it require any specific requirements to be met for that, or any specific form to be met for that? And I am referring to civilians.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As this was the only way for citizens to actually leave outside the territory of the municipality, and go outside the territory of the municipality, when they reported, when they applied for leaving, they actually stated their desired destinations in connection with where their families or their relatives were. A number of citizens from Samac had relatives also in Tuzla and in Sarajevo and in Gradacac. So I'm talking about the southern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And a number of citizens had family in Croatia. But most of them mainly wished to go to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was through Croatia that they very often, in quite significant numbers, in fact, would obtain visas to leave to third countries, and this was something they could not do via the Bosnia and Herzegovina Federation, so that for the most part they wanted to leave through Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Maslic, this particular example of a list that you say was a list, line 8, page 43, in response to a question on that line, on line 10 you say: "These are such lists." I presume you mean this is an example of such a list. But this example has no stamp of the Red Cross and it has no date whatsoever. So we don't have here either a date when these 122 persons applied to the Red Cross and were put on a list, and neither do we have any dates as to when they were assigned to be exchanged. Was that usual, to have no stamps, no dates?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: And no signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to ask the witness to clarify for us that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain to the Judge, to Judge Williams.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not customary for lists to be made without a date, without a number, and without a stamp. I believe that this is just the working part of the list, as it were, which served for practical purposes, for the negotiations with the opposite side. So this is not the final list. Our final list would have to have a stamp and be dually registered in the books.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And another question which stems perhaps from this question of Judge Williams. Would all the persons on this list be exchanged within the same exchange?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a situation where people would change their mind and then --

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were different situations. We had people who applied to leave, applied to the Red Cross to be exchanged. And when the actual exchange was about to take place, they would change their mind. For any reason, either because some of their people, their soldiers, imprisoned soldiers, were not going or because they did not obtain the necessary approval or the letter of guarantee, due to different motives, depending on the actual situation in which these people found themselves in particular circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now you've just said something which I was interested in, in relation to the Republic of Croatia. So irrespective of the fact that the person in question applied to you wanting to be exchanged and that you did not make that exchange of that person conditional upon anything, did the opposite side concretely speaking, the Republic of Croatia, make the entry, the coming of civilians into its territory conditional upon anything? You've just -- I am suggesting, but I wish to expedite matters.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The opposite side had its own requirements also, expressed desires. They said that they wanted to accept or to have family members who had remained here and who the rest of their families were seeking from Croatia. They wanted to -- these people to cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
