utterances.text: This is not what I asked you. You mentioned some letters of guarantee. What was that about?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were letters of guarantee which were brought by either representatives of the Red Cross or by colleagues from the Red Cross organisation in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If a civilian from Samac wanted to go to Croatia and had no letter of guarantee, could you take them there?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could, but only if that person was accepted by the Croatian side, if that person was not wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "the other side," --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. The interpreter is lost because of the overlap between question and answer. Sorry. I did not hear the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can you repeat? And please pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked whether persons who wished to go to Croatia, in connection whether these conditions, permits were also issued inter alia by representatives of the Croatia Defence Council. That was my question. The witness said yes.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document be tendered into evidence? Can I be assigned a number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D96/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe that we had the interpretation. Because, you see, when we heard the intervention from the interpreters, it was about the question on page 46, line 8. When you say "the other side," -- and we still don't have the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was: When you said to the opposite side, what did you mean by the opposite side? Just that. In the relationship between the Serbian side and the Croatian side. What was the opposite side of the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commission on exchanges on their side, the Croatian side, and the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Then again here on page 47, line 5, it is marked as answer, although it was a question posed by the counsel. Just that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you now please tell me something else: You said that you knew that in Samac there had been detainees held in, I shall call them detention units. You mentioned the school, the hotel. Tell me: Do you know whether anyone requested for these persons to be exchanged, whether anyone on the opposite side asked for these detained persons to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Do you know who made the actual decisions on their exchange?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Here on page 47 again on line 18, we see the hotel in the transcript. You mentioned the school, but he didn't mention the hotel. There was no one in the hotel at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just mentioned the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I'll repeat my last question: Do you know who it was that made the decisions on the detainees, whether these detainees could be exchanged or not?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the police and the army who made such decisions, and no one could leave without their permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who it was in the police or in the army who actually made such decisions, and how do you know that fact?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who specifically it was who decided in the army and the police, but I do know that every list of people who were requested and who were in -- who were sought, who were in detention, they had to go there, and they did the checking out in terms whether some people could indeed be exchanged or not, and to establish whether the persons -- whether there were any obstacles in regard to any particular person for that person to leave, to be exchanged. So I don't know in detail who it was by name that made such decisions. I did not inquire. Nor did I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell me: Did you ever go to the Crisis Staff to inform them of anything or to ask for any permission regarding exchanges?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went to the Crisis Staff on that particular score, but as a representative of the Red Cross, it was my obligation to inform the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Did you ever inform or ask for permission from the War Presidency or Municipal Assembly that started functioning in 1993 for people to be exchanged from the territory of Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we only informed the Executive Council, but we never asked for permission from these two bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which two bodies do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you said yourself: The War Presidency and the Municipal Assembly, the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will take a look at some documents that have to do with the decisions of the committee on exchanges. There were several such decisions. Now tell me this, please: When you became president or chairman of the exchange committee, did you inform any of these institutions on exchanges, and what did you inform them about?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this committee was established by the Executive Council, there was an obligation to inform about these activities, just in the form of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We will get back to that once we take a look at these documents. The Prosecutor's microphone is on and I don't know if I'm to expect an objection or not? MR. DI FAZIO: No objection. Perhaps a clarification. Mr. Lukic's questions seem to expressly exclude the Crisis Staff. There's a reference to the Municipal Assembly and the War Presidency, but not the Crisis Staff. Now, that may be intentional. I don't know. If -- in terms of referring back to these authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That question was asked. If you look at page 48, I think, line 21, the witness even answered that: "I never went to the Crisis Staff on that particular score." MR. DI FAZIO: I am sorry. I apologise and I withdraw that comment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And he explained to whom his obligations lay. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry. I missed that, and I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to emphasise this: That this had to do with the time when this witness became chairman of the exchange committee. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, please tell me: During an exchange itself, once you bring in the individuals who were to be exchanged, what happens next? What happens at the crossing line?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every person who, based on his or her expressed wish to cross over to the other side, is put on a list, and then an approval is obtained, and then these persons come to the separation line, and then they had to once again state whether they still wished to cross over to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did they have to state this to?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had to state this to the committee of the opposing side. As far as I know, at every exchange the military committee from Banja Luka required that the International Red Cross be present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they indeed attend every exchange that you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they did not. I don't know what were the reasons behind that, but I know that they attended some exchanges, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were representatives of some other international institution present at various exchanges?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the Trial Chamber is familiar with the fact that we - and here I mean the local Red Cross exchange committee and military committee, as well as exchange committees from other municipalities: Modrica, Derventa, Doboj, Gradiska - went to negotiations to the current Republic of Croatia, which is where the UN forces were, in the area near the highway between Zagreb and Belgrade, the place that is called Dragalic, or Novska, or we went to the other side, to the place called Lipovac, in Serbia. This is some 300 to 400 kilometres from Samac. We went there because that was the only safe place, as we were protected by the UN forces. We were unable to reach an agreement with the opposite side to have that done somewhere closer to us, in Orasje, which is some ten kilometres from Samac. They were unable to provide sufficient security measures for us to be able to negotiate there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Judge Lindholm has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Earlier, during the statement of the witness, he talked about the persons exchanged from Samac over to the other side, what it does mean, I don't exactly know. But then he went on and talked about detained people. Why, and for what purpose, were the persons being object to exchange detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you that, because I don't know why they had been detained. The Red Cross had no information concerning that, no data whatsoever, so I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not reply to Mr. Lukic's question, and with your permission, I will reply now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this was at a certain distance from Samac and that this was under the protection of the UN forces. As far as I remember, there was Jordanian battalion there and the Nepalese one. The soldiers of the UN forces had to get involved every time we contacted the opposing side and enabled us to conduct negotiations unhindered. The vehicles in which the prisoners and civilians were transported were also provided. They attended every exchange, and their sole aim was to provide the necessary security measures during our stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order to explain this to the Trial Chamber, when you say "Dragalic, Lipovac, Novska," what was the other side that you conducted negotiated with, those places?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were negotiations conducted with the representatives of the Croatian Defence Council and with Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it possible to enter these zones under the UN protection while carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, these zones were called UNPA zones, and nobody who was in uniform or wearing weapons was able to enter those zones, even the representatives of military committees had to come there without uniforms and without weapons. Everybody who came there wearing uniform and bearing arms was turned back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it necessary to inform the UN about every entrance into that zone?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of this had to be announced several days prior to that, or at least one or two days prior to that, in order for them to be able to prepare everything and to obtain permissions from their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we will turn to some matters in chronological order. We will now focus on several exchanges. Could the witness be shown document D12/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the exchange that took place in the beginning of June -- no, beginning of July 1992 in Lipovac, which was within the UNPA zone? You will take a look at the list now, and perhaps a name on the list will trigger your memory. Did you attend this particular exchange? Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I was present in the capacity of the Red Cross representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there anything peculiar about this exchange on the 4th of July that made you remember this? Were there any technical problems?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. This exchange was scheduled either on the 4th of July or on the 5th of July. But I believe it was on the 4th of July. We received information from the representatives of the Croatian side that they had some technical problems and that they were unable to bring the detainees from their side. And they asked that we spend the night in Lipovac and that this, according to them, would be done tomorrow, and this is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now please take a look at the name under number 44. There is something else written there next to that name. Could you comment on this, please.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Stipo Vukovic, a man who then, at the site, stated that he did not wish to cross over to the other side, despite the fact that he had been sought by the other side. He stated then that he did not want to cross over, and he was sent back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that man personally? Did he live in Samac later on?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him by sight. I know that he lived in Samac later on and that he came to the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague is reminding me to ask you: Why did he come to the Red Cross later on?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Due to the humanitarian aid that he received.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: When a detained person, be he detained either in Samac or in Batkovici, is brought to the exchange line and then states that he does not wish to be exchanged, is he returned back to the prison or sent back home?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody who stated he did not wish to cross over to the other side was sent back home and continued living as any other free citizen. Mr. Matheas paid special attention to such persons and required the local Red Cross to provide protection to such individuals, just like to any other persons, and this was upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have already told us something about military committees. Tell us this, please: When did you learn that there was a republic committee for exchanges, and did you have any contacts with this committee at the republic level?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the republic level?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We will turn to the military commission later on.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the republic commission existed in 1993, although we had very few contacts with it, and they did not put in any requests to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: When were the first contacts established with military commissions? Who did you get to know there? And tell us briefly: How was the cooperation established, and why was the cooperation needed between the military and the civilian commissions? You've mentioned the 1st Krajina Corps, but tell us: When did the cooperation start?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the corridor was severed, it was possible to come to Samac from Modrica, Doboj, and Derventa, Gradiska, and Dragalic. This was a road that we took to go to negotiations with Croats. So after the corridor was penetrated in Modrica, shortly thereafter, Captain Milutin Grujicic came to Samac and introduced himself as president or chairman of the military commission for exchanges within the 1st Krajina Corps. At the time, he talked with us about the Red Cross and told us about the possibility to meet with the representatives of the Croatian military commission and the Croatian Red Cross. We were mostly interested in our colleagues from the Red Cross in Orasje, Brod, Odzak, and even in Gradiska. We were interested in establishing contact with them. I believe that it was sometime in late July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before these direct contacts that you had with the opposing side, how was the contact established between these two sides?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the only available contact was through the radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? Do you mean the communications centre, centre for reporting?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because there is a radio station in Samac as well, but that is a different entity; is that right? When was the first time you went to communications centre? Can you specify that for us?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember when it was that I went there, but I believe that I only went to the commissions centre a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And later on, when direct contacts were established with the opposing side, when negotiations started, was this contact through communications centre still in use?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, because it was a complicated way to communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the document D64/3 be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You referred yesterday to your contacts and cooperation with the military commission. What is this before you? Will you say -- tell us in a few words.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a specific request addressed by Mr. Grujicic, sent by Mr. Grujicic, and I believe it is to the command of the United Nations forces, telling them that this group would go there for negotiations and with what vehicles they would come, and other pertinent information. Because unless you provided such particulars, one could not enter the UNPA zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the persons on this list. Here we can see your name, as well as one of Tadic's name. Are the other persons here just military personnel, or are there any civilians on this list? Why are these people on this list? What jobs did they do?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this list there are representatives of the military commission, or rather, the military commissions, as well as of civilian commissions. There are people from Samac, from Modrica, from Derventa, and from Brcko, at Bijeljina. Specifically, if I need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, there is no need. Just a minute. Just one minute. Correction. Page 57, line 9. And from Bijeljina. And from Bijeljina also. I'm just interested in a particular individual on this list, because I believe he will feature in the case. Who is the person under serial number 5 and why is that person on the list? What was his job?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Maksim Simeunovic, Captain First Class by rank, member of the commission of exchanges of the East Bosnia Corps, a man from Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was his nickname Maksa?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, Mr. Maslic: At the negotiations themselves, did you, as representatives of the civilian -- could you, as representatives of the civilian commissions, interfere in the work of the military commissions and their representatives who were conducting the negotiations? Could you decide or could you advise them as to the forming of their opinions?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian commission could not at all make any decisions, especially not in terms of any military issues, nor did it have any such powers in respect of these negotiations. We cooperated with the military commission primarily in terms of our being of service to them in order to provide them with particulars and data from our respective areas from which we hailed, as I say, Samac, Modrica, et cetera. I'm talking about the information about the captured persons, the missing persons, and all other persons who were pertinent whose families came to the Red Cross. The people, the families, could not go to Banja Luka, but the data, descriptions of the soldiers, photographs of the soldiers, is something that they provided and we also provided this service to them in order to help the members of the families to indeed find the person that they were looking for as part of this exchange process.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify this. Did you give the military commissions any information about the detainees?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They got these -- such information from the units from which the soldiers went missing. As I said, we gave such information to the families or from the families we gather information which was material for that particular soldier to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the military commission submit any information to you about the civilians that were being sought? Did you have any such situations in your work?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military commissions sometimes asked that we -- asked us to try and bring a civilian, the member of whose family was to be exchanged as a soldier and lived in our municipality. This is in respect of this, they submitted their requests to us, and in the process we always abided by this requirement of family reunification, unless we have a situation where the soldier in question was to be exchanged and the family would remain, so in this sense they sent us their requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the document please be shown; document D5/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: While finding that document, I would like to ask perhaps my memory doesn't serve me quite correctly, but first the witness told us that the persons being exchanged from Bosnia-Herzegovina were prisoners of war, and then that they were detainees. And I understand that they were civilians. My third, following up that, why were they detained in order to be exchanged? I haven't got any answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness explained that he didn't know why people had been detained in Samac. I don't think he ever mentioned that people were detained in order to be exchanged. He never said anything of the kind. I believe that these two matters are wholly unassociated. But I shall ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, the detention of persons, did it have anything to do with the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said I don't know why people were detained, and their detention has nothing, their capturing has nothing whatsoever to do with exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bear with me, please. I don't know whether this is a satisfactory reply for Judge Lindholm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: No, it isn't, because you were so much involved in this process, it's unexplainable that you didn't know why they were detained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that, as an activist of the Red Cross and a representative of the Red Cross, I dealt exclusively with humanitarian work and the problems associated with humanitarian work, so that I could not have known, nor did I know the reasons why any person had been detained or imprisoned or captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go on. Did you have any -- take any part of exchanges of persons not being detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Persons who were not detained were not exchanged. They simply crossed over to the other side together with the -- when some members of their families were being exchanged. So nor did the opposite side ask for these people to be actually exchanged just to make it possible for them to cross over from either side. So persons and civilians crossed from either side on this basis. The exchange process referred and covered exclusively soldiers who were detained, and not civilians who crossed in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you draw up lists of civilians who went along with -- who were also exchanged?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These lists had to be made on the basis of requests coming from these civilians themselves and the request of the opposite side, in order to enable for them to leave the territory of the municipality without any hindrance, because there were checkings and the police controlled every exit from the municipality, and the police then authorised or gave its permission to such lists, and that is why these lists were compiled in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Could civilians enter an UNPA zone without there having been drawn a list which was to be submitted to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before any entrance into the zone, a list had to be previously submitted, and the United Nations troops would examine the list, and very often they would actually collate, control, the detained soldiers and the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To follow up on the question posed by Judge Lindholm, in respect of the detainees, you said that as a member of the Red Cross you couldn't know. Did you know that there were any rebellions in Samac regarding -- in connection with illegal arming? Have you heard of any procedures?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that there had been some proceedings instituted, but as a humanitarian worker I was not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take a brief look at this document. I will repeat this question, because I don't believe the answer is in the trial record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My last question was: Did the military commissions assist you and submit to you any information about the persons being sought? Did you get any such information from them? You recall that I asked you this question. Please briefly answer.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this list. Do you recall this particular exchange? Do you know where it took place? Take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this was -- this exchange was in Dragalici, and I know some of the people on the list, and I know that on that occasion a number of them opted for returning home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The handwritten additions by some names, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that exactly refers to those persons who left, who changed their mind and went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now tell me, please, since we are constantly using the term "exchange": If they left, had anyone come to your side when this exchange took place?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The people on this list left, they left to the other side. Did the other side, did the opposite side bring anyone on that occasion? Whom and from where?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The opposite side always brought a certain number of sought persons, according to these lists, for every exchange, because those lists had been agreed beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember at this specific exchange? Not, of course, by name, but what was the profile? What was the ethnicity of the people who came?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, they were people from Novi Grad, Dubica, Trnjak, this area generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Of what nationality were these people?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Could they -- could they have come of their own, if they wanted to come to the territory of Samac, would these Croatian authorities let them come to your territory, the territory of Samac municipality in an organised fashion, spontaneously, as it were?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were captured there. They were imprisoned. They had been captured and were in prison there and could not come of their own initiative without a formal exchange and the permission to that effect by the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you look at the person under serial number 22. Sorry. 25. 25. Do you recall this person? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the name. Dragan Lukac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He was the chief of the police station in Samac. I know him personally. And I know that on that particular occasion, with his colleague policemen who accompanied him, he was sitting, or he stayed in Gradiska, and they were having drinks there while they were waiting for the exchange to take place. Now, why have I remembered this particular thing? Because the people on the buses reacted to his presence, actually, objected to his presence, because they saw no reason for him to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document which I'd like to be shown to the witness bears the internal mark PDB 82/3. This is a letter from the 27th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please comment on this document.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic is writing to me personally, as the president of the Red Cross, asking me to comply with a request by a colleague of mine from Gradiska, which refers to a civilian who was to have crossed over to the other side, the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did it often happen that military commissions sent each other messages through you, corresponded with each other through you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had a lot of contacts, and during each of these there were requests made to us, and whatever we were able to comply with, we did, in order to enable civilians to cross over if they wished to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D97/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like the witness to be shown documents B83 and B84 [as interpreted]. To speed things up, we can show both documents together. P83.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the documents, Mr. Maslic, these are documents concerning decisions issued by the commission for exchange: When exchanges were carried out, why was it necessary, in October 1992, to issue formal decisions by or on the side of the commissions for exchange?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the issues that arose in the area of the municipality, that is, there was an enormous number of requests for people to go over to the other side, the Executive Board decided to set up a commission to deal with this so that it could be informed of these activities. That was one of the aspects of their work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We just want to be sure what we are looking at. Is it P83 and P84?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We will look at document P83.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is a document issued by the War Presidency, about the establishment of the commission and the appointment of its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were appointed president of the commission?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a representative of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: This other person, who is it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Simo Nikolic, a person who was a soldier. He had some sort of rank in the military, in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What brigade are you referring to? Can you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the 2nd Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how it came about that Tadic was appointed a member of that commission?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was because he knew the Odzak area, and the Serbs taken prisoner in Odzak and the surrounding area, and that was the reason for his appointment, I think. And I don't know whether it's also because he was in the civilian protection staff. I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The two of you had cooperated before that with reference to the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tadic would come to the Red Cross and would do whatever the Red Cross asked him to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you look at Article 3 of this decision, please. I'm interested in knowing whether you yourself, as it says in Article 3, submitted reports to the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't submit any reports to the War Presidency, but we submitted reports to the Executive Board or council, as I have already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the witness please be shown document P84 now. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, you may be helped by an explanation of why reports weren't going to the War Presidency and were going to the Executive Council. The document is clear and plain, but the -- it wasn't being followed. I mean, I know that I can clarify it in cross-examination, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that is a question for cross-examination. MR. DI FAZIO: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this other document now. Is it familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why was this decision issued? Do you know? And who are the persons mentioned in it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These persons were never active members of the commission, and I think the reason for this decision was that the representatives of the municipality of Pelagicevo asked to be included because they also had persons who had been taken prisoner, who came from their municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the documents. I would now ask that the witness be shown document D76/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for this document, would you please tell me: Mr. Simo Nikolic, did he take an active part in the work of the commission for exchanges?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I conclude that in practice it was you and Tadic who actually worked in the commission from the time of its inception? Would you repeat your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document issued by the Executive Council, and it was in fact complied with. Reports were submitted and appointments were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document dates from May 1993. Do you remember that before May 1993 you informed the Executive Council of work on exchanges?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we could take a break now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, you're supposed to finish by 1830, according to the hours for this witness. We'll take a break now and proceed at 1805.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to appeal to the Trial Chamber regarding the information giving me -- by the Presiding Judge as to the time left for this witness. I have to say, Your Honours, that this is one of the key witnesses for the defence of Miroslav Tadic. The second issue is that we were given 70 hours for our witnesses. When I added up viva voce witnesses, I came to a maximum of 42 hours. When I drafted my pre-trial brief, I estimated six to seven hours for this witness. We have several other important topics remaining, such as Zasavica, Batkovici and so on, and the Judges so far have put quite a lot of questions to this witness. I would also like to remind you that Stevan Todorovic was initially expected to testify for two and a half days and remained here for two weeks. This is a very important witness for Miroslav Tadic, for this Trial Chamber, for this trial, because this is a witness that can tell us a lot about exchanges. And I will try to focus on what is most important for us, but I do not believe that I will be able to complete today. I think that I will need another 45 minutes on Monday. I hope the Trial Chamber will grant this request. If you believe that I'm repeating myself and putting the same questions, then I will abide by your ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. The Trial Chamber will give you the time you need, since you say this is your key witness. So you go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, we will now briefly analyse another document, with internal marking PDB --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: PDB --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. Maslic: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You signed it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've told us that Simo Nikolic did not actually work with you, although his name is listed on the document, dated May 1993. The municipal authorities, be it War Presidency or Executive Council, did they comply with your request? Did they grant your request? Were you given an additional member?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please: From the beginning of 1993, was there a War Presidency or another body?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the Executive Council, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the Municipal Assembly start functioning, Municipal Assembly of Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. But I'm still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D97/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: No. 98. MR. DI FAZIO: 98.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 98 maybe.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. D98/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. I'm still interested in some confusing concepts. Here, in this document, the English translation, starting from line 1 in the proper text: "Since the hitherto member of the commission for the exchange of prisoners of war ..." It is still unclear for me what the meaning of "exchange" was, because you have told about -- talked about prisoners of war, detained persons, and other persons. Could you clarify that with this witness so it becomes clear to the Chamber what you are talking about? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, in this letter -- I will read this out to you, because it is not next to you. In the beginning of your letter you are saying as follows: In view of the fact that the member of the commission for exchange of war prisoners, Nikolic Sima, and so on and so forth. You, in your letter, called this commission "commission for exchange of war prisoners." Can you please explain to us what you meant? And why was the commission called "commission for exchange of civilians," and so on?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document itself says "commission for exchange of war prisoners." However, that was not the role of this commission. We simply took over the name from the military commissions. This was not in fact a commission for exchange of war prisoners. It was simply a customary name used in other municipalities, although this commission was not involved in exchange of war prisoners. The official name of this nature belongs to the military commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to add another explanation to Judge Lindholm: Do you know that Croatian commission also had in its name prisoners of war and arrested civilians?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And we simply took over the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And was this commission used or involved in getting the Serb civilians to cross over to the other side?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And just conclude for the benefit of Judge Lindholm. The commission in which you and Miroslav Tadic worked in, was it ever involved in exchange of war prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was never involved in exchange of war prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Well, I have a follow-up question, perhaps depending on the country I come from. Wasn't it possible for civilians to cross the border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia without any official procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that this is a very relevant question of Judge Lindholm. Could you please clarify this.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would be most happy if it was possible to do it in this way and to have citizens cross over from both sides unhindered, because that would be the simplest and the best way. However, due to the war and the combat that was going on, that was impossible. The only possible way was our way. The only bridge across the Sava River between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia was located in Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we will turn to another topic. Have you heard of the village of Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us about that village? Is there anything peculiar concerning it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That village is some seven kilometres from Samac, next to the Bosna River. It's a village mostly populated by Croats. This village was never shelled during the war, unlike other villages and the town itself, which were shelled daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The nearby villages around Zasavica, were they shelled?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The village of Crkvina is a neighbouring village, and it was shelled daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were the shells coming from?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that they were fired from Orasje, from the Republic of Croatia, from that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether a group of individuals was accommodated in an organised way in the village of Zasavica in autumn of 1992? Do you know who found housing for those people there, and why?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that some residents from the town, residents of Croat and Muslim nationality, were housed in that village, whereas the original residents of the village were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who took them to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was done by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Do you know how many people were brought into Zasavica at the time? What was their gender and age profile?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact figure, but I believe that there were women and children there, as well as men. There were different people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know why they were brought there?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know, was there anything characteristic about Zasavica? Was there something at the entry point into the village?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the entrance into the village there was a police guard, there were guards there who controlled the traffic in and out of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Did you personally ever visit Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Zasavica once with Mr. Matteas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "once," can you try and recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning, after these people had been taken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not specific enough. Can you remember when those people had been taken there?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what month it was?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there with Mr. Matteas, who asked that we go there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I will have to interrupt you. Is that Matteas from the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Matteas who was a delegate of the International Red Cross, who asked that we go there together to see what were the living conditions of those people. And we planned some joint activities in order to assist those people and create better living conditions for them. I accepted his proposal. We went there together and we established contact with the commissioner of that local commune, Mr. Ivica Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I have a --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a break here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: No, not a break, but a question. When you talk about that place and you say: "Together to see where the living conditions of those people," what do you mean by the expression "those people"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had in mind both the residents of the Zasavica local commune who had lived there before and those who had been brought there by police. And when I said "living conditions," I meant the food, the clothing, medications, and everything else that they needed, because they were unable to leave the village without permits, without bypassing the police. Somebody had to bring in the food and the aid to them, and that was the responsibility of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. There were permanent inhabitants in that village. I'm right? And then you have the detained persons in facilities I don't want to mention. Of whom are you now speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to the residents of the local commune of Zasavica who had lived there before the war also, and to people that the police had brought from Samac who were put up in the houses there, put in the houses, not in detention, not in prison; in the houses in the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I must ask you a further question. You say "in the houses of the village." Where were they kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commissioner of the local commune, the local community of Zasavica, Mr. Ivica Pandurevic, told us that together with several villagers, he had put up these people into different houses where there was space for these people to be accommodated, and Pandurevic himself has a large, spacious house, into which he took in two or three families, which could live there quite normally. So it was not a prison in that house or in those houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have given us quite detailed explanation, but let us exhaust this story of Zasavica. You referred to the commissioner of this local commune, Mr. Pandurevic? What is a commissioner? Did such functions exist elsewhere, and what kind of a contact did your service have with such persons holding these posts?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every local community in the area of the municipality had its local community commissioner, which was man number one in the village, in other words, who represented the village in question, who came to the Municipal Assembly, to the Red Cross organisation, to the health centre, as the case was maybe, and sought the assistance he required for his village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What nationality was Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have frequent contacts, you personally, with him during the war?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had very frequent contacts with Mr. Pandurevic, and everything which was necessary for the villagers of his village, he came to get at the Red Cross, and he got the assistance required, according to the criteria which had already been defined. Also at his request we set up a clinic, an infirmary there, in order to provide medical care to the population which was living there at the time. I believe that a physician went to the infirmary once a week to be on duty there, and as appropriate, he would also go there more often if the need arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please finish this story of the visit, of your visit with Mr. Matteas. What happened then? Did you have any further talks on the subject? What happened on that occasion? Please explain.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally accompanied Mr. Matteas, went with him to Zasavica. We came to Mr. Pandurevic's home. He asked me to let him talk in my absence to the people who were there, who had come there, after he saw the vehicle of the International Red Cross. Now, what they had actually talked about, I don't know, because he asked me to -- for him to talk himself individually with all the persons who were there, and I indeed saw that he talked to some of those people, Muslims and Croats, those that had been brought from Samac as well as those who lived there originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: What do you know, since you say that Zasavica had never been shelled during the war, so tell me: What do you know about the situation with water and electricity, and generally life, or living conditions in that village, in comparison to Samac?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards water, this village had a very well-constructed artesian well with potable water, in other words, and as for electricity, I believe that it was supplied with electricity, just like all the other villages in the area of the municipality. So I believe that the conditions relative to the situation in the city itself were much safer and much better. In terms of the shelling and given the uncertainty that the shelling and the firing entailed for the citizens of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the witness be shown document internally marked D0017, please. This is a document that was introduced at one point by the Prosecution -- by the Defence - sorry - of Mr. Simic. It is dated the 29th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm familiar with this document. I signed it. And this document, or rather, this letter, with this letter, I addressed the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly, with the request for them to provide a certain quantity of food for us. You can see in the letter that there were 245 people living there at the time. So I'm asking for a certain quantity of flour, given the fact that the Red Cross was unable to supply such flour, according to the request of Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Do you remember now the date when these people -- you said you don't remember the date when these people were brought. Did this number of 245 people include both the inhabitants of Zasavica and those who had been brought there then?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This number refers to them all, the total figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So at the time of this letter, these people had already been brought to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that was the reason why I asked for additional quantities of food for that particular community, because I could not meet the requirements, the request of Mr. Pandurevic, according to certain already defined criteria.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. Could you read out -- this is a very short letter, but could you read it out or get it into English? I understand that it's a question of 245 people, but it would be interesting to know the exact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. I think the problem with the 245 is that it appears in the B/C/S version, but a line has been left out in the English translation. There are -- after Zasavica, MZ Zasavica in the B/C/S version, there's a full stop and then there's another sentence with the population figure in. That sentence beginning: "U [phoen] Zasavica," et cetera, is missing in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be best if I were to read out this letter, after all, for your benefit, so that it could be interpreted. Or perhaps the witness could read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Maslic, take the document in your hand and read it slowly. Tell us -- so subject --

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Subject of the letter is provision of flour for the inhabitants of Zasavica, we request -- we are addressing you with this letter, asking you to approve (supply or provide) 1 tonne of flour for the needs of the population, of the inhabitants of the local community of Zasavica." Full stop. "There are currently accommodated in Zasavica 245 inhabitants of different ages --"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe that this sufficiently clarifies this point. I believe that it is okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're waiting for the number. If the registrar will kindly assign us one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D99/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: You mentioned this yesterday, and let us amplify a bit on this subject now. You said that there was heavy influx of refugees into the territory of Samac municipality. What was the role of the Red Cross in respect of those refugees? Were any records made? Were these records submitted to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the document D46/3 please be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said at the very outset, in the beginning of my statement, that prior to the outbreak of war in the area of Samac municipality, there had been accommodated in our territory a number of refugees that had come from the Republic of Croatia from war-ridden areas in that republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We know all this. But please, to expedite matters, could you be more specific, more concrete? Did you have larger influxes of refugees, et cetera, some more specific information?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already at the end of 1993, people started coming from the commune of Odzak, from the municipality of Odzak, and other municipalities, and the number of refugees grew daily, of refugees, people who had relatives or family in our municipality and wished to remain there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a problem, a technical problem, because the witness was able to hear the English interpretation, just as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You may continue now.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, in late 1992 a commissariat for aid to refugees and humanitarian aid was set up, because the Red Cross organisation was unable to carry out the entire job of registering refugees and taking care of the refugees arriving in the municipality, which is why a special service was set up, which was called the commissariat for refugees and humanitarian aid. Mr. Milorad Mihajlovic was appointed commissioner, and there was another person working with him. Their premises were in the Red Cross, but they took over only that part of the work which consisted in registering refugees. At the level of Republika Srpska, there were forms --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We needn't go into detail.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and the forms contained information on the name of the refugee, where they had come from, why they had arrived, where they were accommodated, where they were living now. The commissariat collected this information and delivered it to the UNHCR on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please just comment on this document? Would you look at the date and say whether after this date the number of refugees grew or declined.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document shows the number of refugees who had already arrived in the Samac municipality and the breakdown by age of these refugees. This information was needed because humanitarian organisations, the ones that provided aid - that was the International Red Cross, the UNHCR, the World Health Organisation - they required this information. This information was contained in forms provided by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... any more, the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Your question was not answered whether, as from the date of that document, the number of refugees in fact increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wishing to expedite matters, I forgot. After this report mentioning some 6.000 refugees in the autumn of 1992, after that, did the number of refugees increase, and until when did this trend continue?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of refugees grew daily. And as far as I know, in 1994 or 1995, in the Samac municipality, there were about 10.000 refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Do you know when the detainees -- just one more question about refugees. Have you heard of the village of Cernica, and do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cernica is a village in the Gradacac municipality, which is about 30 kilometres away from Samac, and it was controlled by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did all the inhabitants of that village cross over to your municipality, and when?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992 we were informed in the Red Cross that an organised group of about 186 families from Cernica were on their way to Samac, and these families were of Serb ethnicity. What we heard in the Red Cross was that they had been allowed to leave and set out in whatever direction they wanted, and they wanted to go to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And were they accommodated on the territory?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Cross and the commissariat for refugees, that is, our activists, received the refugees, provided the basic necessities, and they stayed in the municipality of Samac and lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember when the detainees, that is, the persons detained in the TO and the schools, when they were transferred to Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact time, but I know that the time they spent in Samac was brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, can you tell us what Batkovic was? It has already been mentioned in this case. We know it's a village, but can you tell us something about it? Where is it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it's a village in the municipality of Bijeljina, about 90 kilometres away from Samac. It's a village where there was a prison for soldiers, and it was controlled by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who gave approval for a person from Batkovic to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was military commissions who asked for that approval, and it was the military authorities that gave it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, as a civilian commission -- or rather, were you able to ask for someone from Batkovici to be exchanged or to take someone from Batkovici to be exchanged without the approval of the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian commission never had this authority, and we were not able to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that someone from the civilian commissions ever went to Batkovici and at whose request -- and at whose orders?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Mr. Tadic, on the request of the military commission from the 1st Corps, with the approval of the military authorities, went to Batkovic to bring detainees in a bus. As far as I know, this was done for technical reasons, because there are about 90 kilometres, as I said, between Batkovici and Samac, and from Samac to Dragalici, or Novska, there are 300 to 400 kilometres. So that on that occasion, as far as I can remember, Tadic brought the detainees as far as Samac, in a bus. They spent the night there on the premises, I think, of the Territorial Defence Staff. And in the morning they were taken in the same bus, with a police escort, to be exchanged in Dragalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will come back to that exchange. Did you ever go to Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went to Batkovici. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, the witness has referred to technical reasons being the reason why Mr. Tadic had to go and collect these prisoners of war or military detainees, whereas he was working in the civilian commission. That evidence won't mean much to you unless you know what technical reasons it was that compelled him to go to Batkovici given all the rest of the evidence in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Can the witness tell us the technical reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know why this request was made from the military authorities for Tadic to go and get the detainees?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it was a technical reason because someone had to go from Banja Luka to Bijeljina, and in order to arrive in Dragalic at 1.00 from Bijeljina and to pass from Bijeljina to Dragalic, they would have to undertake a journey of 400 kilometres. And along that route, they would be stopped at some ten or so checkpoints. So they would have had to travel all night in order to arrive in time. And as I said, it was only 90 kilometres away, and that was the technical reason why Mr. Tadic did this at the request of the military commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On those occasions when military prisoners were taken for exchange, and also citizens from Samac were to be exchanged, did you ever go?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, in almost every exchange that took place, civilians were also exchanged, and then the families of the soldiers who had come from Batkovici would join in the exchange and go with them, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask that the following documents be put before the witness: D13, D13/3, that is, and D14/3. They can be shown to the witness together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that representatives of other civilian commissions with whom you cooperated also went to Batkovici at the request of military representatives? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that representatives from the Modrica municipality went there also, but I don't know anything specific about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These are two letters. Would you please tell us to whom the first one was addressed, to whom the second one was addressed, and what these documents refer to.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This first document -- when you say the first, can you tell us what the number is and can you tell us to whom it was addressed?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was addressed to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, to Mr. Zdravko Tolimir personally, on Pale, and it was sent by Mr. Milutin Grujicic, the president of commission for exchanges of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the date?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 1st of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see any of your fellow townspeople on this list?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This other letter, what date does it bear, and can you comment on it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was also sent by Mr. Milutin Grujicic. He was the president of the commission for exchanges of the 1st Krajina Corps. And he addressed it to the command of the East Bosnian Corps. As far as I can recall, Colonel Pero Jakovljevic was the security officer of the corps, and he asked him to make it possible for the prisoners on the list to be exempt, or to be separated out. And it's evident from the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that your commission organised for their families to accompany those people from Samac? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the families did go. I know that the family of Zaimbegovic Esref went, and another person's family.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of what happened to these people when they were taken from Batkovici to Samac and then to Dragalic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that when they spent the night in Samac, that they were mistreated and beaten by the police. And when they went to be exchanged, some of them had visible injuries resulting from the beatings. Mr. Tadic and Grujicic intervened because of this, through the police, and also they intervened with the army leaders, because it was inappropriate for that to be done to those people. Grujicic informed me of that at the exchange, and so did Mr. Tadic. And I think that there is a document which shows that Grujicic suggested very strongly that he condemned this action.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it is time to break. I can promise that I will be very brief on Monday, but I would not be able to pinpoint the exact time I will take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. We shall adjourn and continue our proceedings on Monday at 0900 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 20th day of January 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
